title: Show HN: Korosta – Remember and highlight job postings you've seen
text:
# What is and whats not

Korosta is a privacy-first user-customizable tool to highlight job postings based on how frequent are those, and your ratings: * how often the job postings appeared to the user -> fade repeatedly seen job postings * learns from your ratings with a simple local model -> highlight relevant ones * 2 versions: free and pro * almost everything is kept local (ratings, recipes, customizations, history), only licensing and payments require a server * no account required to use it (just when doing the purchase)

This is not a job tracker, job board, or automated application system. It just annotates what you already have visible in your browser's tab.

## Links

chrome: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/korosta/dhpnogbefak... firefox: https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/korosta/

Howto create recipes fast (With the help of a LLM): https://covatools.com/korosta/howtos/create-cookbook-with-an... Website (with ultra short videos): https://korosta.app

# Why

This idea started like 2 years ago, when I was laid off from a tech company (2024's common rounds), and I started the stressful job searching. For job searching, my main platform was, and still is, linkedin: I perfected my url parameters so I can easily have my 10 different tabs. But one questions that commonly had, was "Have I already seen this job post?", and honestly, I wont be saving manually every item in a tool like trello (or the new ones). That question plus my bad memory had me with: "that role is awesome!!! ohhh I already seen it... but 2 months ago" (something like job posting recycling? maybe).

The main objective of this tool/extension is to reduce the load / fatigue of remembering what you have already seen (and not in just a single site), and also highlight what could be interesting to you personally (by learning with your ratings) -> less time searching, and thus, giving more time to apply in the relevant ones, or doing something else (like recovering your energy).

One thing I also spent time around was in the customization / editor (+ the howto in the page), so almost anybody can extend the tool (recipes/cookbook) <- I get frustrated when I love a tool but I fully depend on the developer

# beyond the technical part (more context... you can skip it, and test already)

Around 16.5 years ago I wanted to develop and sell apps, like the trend in those days... I did not. One year ago, I was thinking the same with the first version, the tool was working (even though over engineered), but I got discouraged by myself by reading all the terms of services, legal + fiscal topics, all the things that I did not know... plus some sites are very aggressive with their terms of use and tools like this.

I got a job, then changed my career path to a contractor, and meanwhile I started looking for a job again, but since the end of 2025 I really understand the new difficulties of the job market + not being sooo young, so I took the previous tool, refurbished it but with a different mindset: customization first with a simple learning algorithm so it can highlight interesting jobs to the user -> the name of the tool "Korosta" means highlight in Finnish (its difficult to find a good name ha).

I do think that is even more relevant to release it now because of AI: some platforms are pushing heavily their AI-based search engines, that are not so easy yet to customize -> putting more stress / burden on us.

In terms of monetization, I defined it based on: I am not keen of subscriptions, I grew up with shareware (like Doom... you can guess my age now), and when a single payment give you something (I wont distribute this in floppies, though). And it ended like: pay once and keep for the same major version.

I learned a lot, and I am still learning, with this development, so I want to hear your comments. Also, If you are looking for a job right now, how does the extension feel to use?

Confession time.

I used to be prone to giving things slightly silly names, particularly unrecoverable structured exceptions. Examples include PancakeLandingException, ReallyBadException, CataclysmicException, ApocalypticDeathException, and the like.

And then years and years ago I used to work for a company called Redgate and I started a tradition of slightly silly messages when early access builds of our .NET products would expire, all based on Monty Python sketches and quotes. So, obviously, the dead parrot sketch featured in there.

So far, so harmless, but this did come to a head somewhat spectacularly and in a couple of different ways.

Firstly, in 2009 one of my colleagues used a modified quote from The Life of Brian as an expiry message on a build. Somebody who appeared to be some sort of religious zealot complained loudly to the company. We were both in LA at the time, with a couple of other colleagues, attending build 2009, so we woke up to a chain of something like 50 panicked emails in our inboxes with people expressing differing levels of outrage and/or amusement whilst discussing various grovelling apology options... until someone figured out that it was actually an elaborate troll that we'd swallowed hook, line, and sinker. I can't remember the name of the person who caught us out but, hats off, well played, sir, well played. It did unfortunately mean we became a bit more cautious and business-like with our early access build expiry messages.

Secondly, and this one needs a bit of context setting... I've always been a fan of descriptive and explicit error messages: there should be enough information in any error message that most of the time the user can figure out what's wrong and fix their own problem OR at least so that if they get in touch with support, then support can quickly figure out the problem and get back to them with a solution. I'm not a fan of unhelpful, information poor, obfuscatory, or cryptic error messages.

But when I wanted to cause an application to exit because there'd been an error related to tampering with our licensing code I played somewhat against type. I wanted error messages that would uniquely identify what had happened, making it easy for us to figure out, whilst giving the user no clue (because I wanted to make it very slightly harder for hackers/crackers - but let's be real: this would never have actually stopped anyone). So I used successive lines of dialogue from a scene in House where House is trying to guess who Wilson's girlfriend is. I have no clear recollection of why I chose this dialogue to reproduce, but... I did.

Anyway, this did lead to some slightly confused support requests coming in from users mostly trying to use the tools legitimately in slightly unusual scenarios, but nothing that was overly burdensome. That was until early 2011, when Greg Young - he of event sourcing fame - posted the following gist because he'd encountered an error that said, "Because I wanna ask you about your girlfriend. I must know who she is, or you would've told me her name.": https://gist.github.com/gregoryyoung/871736.

Not at all creepy, right? And, of course, it went viral on twitter. Cue another massive email thread although, this time round, people just thought it was funny. However, we did decide to make the error messages a bit more boring and, in the end, I just gave them numbers.

Mostly I'm just glad the error Greg got wasn't the final line of dialogue in the exchange between House and Wilson: "Yo mamma." That would have been bad.

title: Open source software is slowly turning into open slop software
text:
Code has become extremely cheap to produce, if you have a 5x claude subscription, you can produce or at least try to produce any piece of software you want. And, to be honest, I actually like that, I feel more people should build their own tools and release them as open source because everyone gets to turn their ideas into real products, for their own use if not for others.

But this also means it is getting easier to copy a product, put it on public GitHub and announce you've killed the paid version. Being open source shouldn't give you a pass for shipping slop. If you are calling your tool a replacement for something people pay for, show how it compares.

In the past week, each time I opened X, I kept seeing ads about a new open source code review tool claiming to be the "CodeRabbit killer". I have used CodeRabbit in the past and it definitely has its shortcomings, but if you're claiming you've killed a product, there needs to be evidence.

I saw the advertisement so many times that I decided to evaluate how the product actually performs, it also gave me an excuse to add review capabilities into my own open source tool called shadowclone which helps me manage my agent skills and ensure that regardless of the harness or model I use, agents consistently follow my engineering preferences.

I ran an eval using Greptile, OpenQodex (the open source tool I wanted to evaluate), and my own implementation of a code reviewer in shadowclone, which is basically a code review skill, a local reviewer and a Github bot that can review on the cloud.

My bot reported a higher proportion of findings that both model judges considered real, but it missed 4 real bugs that Greptile caught and as for OpenQodex, I will let the results speak for themselves.

1. Greptile found 69% of the known bugs and 68% of its findings were judged as real 2. shadowclone cloud bot found 38% and 96% of the findings were judged as real 3. shadowclone locally found 36% and 91% of the findings were judged as real 4. OpenQodex found 31% and 86% of its findings were judged as real

The local reviewers ran 3 times per PR. You can see the full eval results at https://github.com/theonly1me/shadowclone/tree/main/evals/code-review

The harness is open source too and you can re-run the eval if you like.

I still want more people to build and release their own tools. I am doing it too. But, if you advertise yours as a replacement for an existing product, I want to see what you tested and where it falls short. Mine missed bugs Greptile caught and publishing that gives me something useful to work on, calling it a Greptile killer wouldn't.
